newsitem.title: FRANCE: French election is scapegoat Juppe's trial by fire.
newsitem.headline: French election is scapegoat Juppe's trial by fire.

text.p: For conservative French Prime Minister Alain Juppe, Sunday's parliamentary election is a personal trial by fire as well a crucial test of his leadership.

To his dismay, the ballot Juppe hoped would produce a vote of confidence for five years of bold action by his centre-right government has been turned, to some extent, into a referendum on his own record and future.

Opinion polls published before last weekend's deadline suggest a close contest in the May 25/June 1 election, with the ruling coalition still favourite but the opposition left within reach of an upset victory.
The same surveys showed fewer than 10 percent of voters want Juppe reappointed if the right wins.
That combined with polls last year showing him to be France's least popular post-war prime minister have made Juppe the favourite whipping boy of both anxious allies and political opponents.
Leftists, warning against "five more years of Juppe", paint him as the embodiment of austerity and tax rises, aimed at helping France qualify for a single European currency.
Several fellow rightists have urged conservative President Jacques Chirac to jettison Juppe as a liability, sniping at his prickly campaign leadership and flawed programme for France.

Juppe, 51, who heads Chirac's Gaullist Rally for the Republic party as well as the government, was viewed as a man of great promise when he was elevated to the Hotel Matignon office in May 1995 after two years as an admired foreign minster.

Two years later, he has become the focus of voters' anger over record high unemployment, public spending cuts, wage freezes for state workers, persistent labour unrest, welfare cut-backs and general grumbling over unkept Chirac campaign promises.
Then there is his image problem.
The slim, balding premier is widely seen as a cold and hard-driving technocrat, uncaring about ordinary citizens.
After his approval ratings sank to post-war record lows, Juppe tried to remedy the problem through public relations.

He had himself photographed in glossy magazines with his wife and infant daughter and penned a short but emotional book, "Entre Nous" (Between Ourselves), in which he admitted to feeling wounded by constant criticism.
He said he had been driven to write by a woman in Bordeaux, where he is mayor, who shouted "Death to idiots" at him in the street.
During the campaign, he has tried to take on critics more directly, often with a poignant touch of self-mockery.
"Would it be better if I were a fat, jovial man unfamiliar with the problems, or someone who was dry and perhaps a bit less jovial but who knew them well," he said in a radio interview.
Asked whether he was stung by constant attacks, he replied: "Everyone says I'm an insensitive computer, so I don't know why you're asking."
Possibly preparing an escape hatch for himself in case he is sacked, Juppe has alternately hinted he would be glad to leave government and happy to stay on after the election.
Chirac has kept silent about his intentions, although insiders say he would like to reappoint Juppe.

The ambiguity has prompted opposition Socialist leader Lionel Jospin to accuse the coalition of playing "cynical games" by trying to fool voters into thinking the president would dump Juppe after the election when he intended to keep him.

A loyal Chirac lieutenant for almost two decades, Juppe's honeymoon with voters fizzled in late 1995 when the president abandoned campaign pledges to cut unemployment and heal social divisions and said cutting public deficits was the top priority.

Born in southwesterly Mont-de-Marsan of modest origins, Juppe attended the elite Ecole Nationale d'Administration (ENA) civil service college before joining Chirac first as a speechwriter in his last weeks as premier in 1976.
Early in the campaign, he suggested it was time for the oft-criticised ENA to be replaced. He later backed down.
